name: Ancient Greek music
sound: Single-line song to lyre or aulos, rhythm set by the poetry's long and short syllables; heard today only in scholarly reconstructions.
markers: One melody line, voice doubled by lyre or reed pipe

Modal scales with unusual small intervals

Chromatic harmony and sudden key shifts
Large orchestra or virtuoso solo piano

Consonant harmony, mallets, keyboards, small ensemble

Solo voice with lyre

Rebetiko and Ottoman-derived modes
Dramatic, heartfelt vocals

name: Turkish pop
sound: Western-style pop sung in Turkish, often with Turkish melodic turns and percussion.
markers: Pop song structure and production
Turkish lyrics with makam-tinged melody
Darbuka or Turkish percussion in the mix

name: Modern Arabic pop (al-jeel)
sound: Arabic pop of the 1980s on: short songs, dance rhythms and Western production around Arabic melody.
markers: Short pop songs, not long tarab suites
Dance and Mediterranean rhythms
Arabic vocals over synths and guitars

name: Marabi and kwela
sound: South African township music: marabi keyboard and dance bands, then kwela pennywhistle jive.
markers: Repeating cyclic chord pattern
Pennywhistle or keyboard lead
Jive and swing rhythms

name: Mande dance-band pop
sound: West African dance bands that electrified griot music, often with Cuban rhythms and horns.
markers: Griot vocal lines and melodies
Electric guitars and horns
Afro-Cuban and Mande dance rhythms

name: Newly composed folk (novokomponovana)
sound: Newly written songs in Balkan folk style for radio and records, with accordion and pop production.
markers: Accordion and clarinet leads
Folk melodies in pop arrangements
Love and village-nostalgia lyrics

name: Japanese art music (koto, shamisen, shakuhachi)
sound: Japanese chamber music for koto, shamisen and shakuhachi, from Edo-period schools to modern composers.
markers: Plucked koto or shamisen, or breathy shakuhachi
Free or slowly unfolding rhythm
Pentatonic Japanese scales

name: Mesoamerican ritual music (conch, flutes, teponaztli)
sound: Ritual music of the Olmec, Maya and Aztec worlds for temple, dance and war: conch trumpets, clay flutes and whistles, the slit-drum teponaztli and the huehuetl, surviving in indigenous dances with chirimía and drum.
markers: Conch blasts and clay flutes
Two-tone teponaztli slit drum and deep huehuetl
Long repeated dance patterns

name: Kalevala runosong (runolaulu)
years: c. 500 onward (ancient oral tradition; written down from 1797, recorded from 1905)
sound: Finnic oral epic and lyric song in unrhymed, alliterative four-foot trochaic Kalevala metre, a short narrow melody repeated line after line, often sung by a lead singer answered by a second.
markers: One short melody repeated for every line of a long story
Unrhymed lines of about eight syllables, heavy alliteration
Call and response or a lead singer echoed, often unaccompanied or with kantele

name: Qur'anic recitation (tilawa) and the call to prayer
sound: Unaccompanied melodic recitation of the Qur'an under the rules of tajwid, from the slow, ornate mujawwad style to the plainer murattal; the adhan calls the faithful to prayer.
markers: One unaccompanied voice
Long held vowels and nasal resonance set by tajwid
Phrases shaped in maqam, separated by long pauses

name: Georgian polyphonic singing
sound: Unaccompanied three-part singing from Georgia: two high voices weave over a drone or moving bass, in close, hard-edged harmony, for the table, the field and the church.
markers: Three unaccompanied voice parts
Drone or moving bass under ornate top lines
Close, dissonant harmony; yodel (krimanchuli) in the west

name: Ngoma (East African drum and dance)
sound: Scope chosen: ngoma in the drum-and-dance sense in Tanzania and coastal Kenya, i.e. community dance music led by sets of tuned hand or stick drums with rattles and call-and-response singing (not the later band genres that borrowed the word).
markers: Several drums of different pitch interlocking, often a bass drum under small goblet drums
Rattles, bells or metal rings keeping a steady pulse
A lead singer answered by a dancing chorus

name: Amazigh ahwash and ahidus
sound: Collective Amazigh village song and dance from the Atlas: two choruses answering each other in lines or circles, over frame drums (bendir/tallunt) and clapping, in Tashelhit (ahwash, High and Anti-Atlas) or Tamazight (ahidus, Middle and eastern High Atlas).
markers: Two large choruses, often men and women, singing antiphonally
Many frame drums and handclaps building interlocking, accelerating rhythms
Dancers shoulder to shoulder in a line or circle led by a central leader

name: Chèo
sound: Northern Vietnamese village folk theatre: bright, nasal solo voices sing folk-derived melodies and comic declamation over fiddles, moon lute, flute and a small drum that sets the pace.
markers: Small chèo drum and clappers driving and punctuating each phrase
Two-string nhị fiddles, đàn nguyệt and sáo answering the singer
Switches between sung melody and half-spoken declamation (nói lệch, nói sử)

name: Ca trù
sound: Intimate northern Vietnamese sung poetry: a woman's tight, throaty, ornamented voice over the buzzing three-string đàn đáy lute, her own phách clappers and a listener's praise drum.
markers: Constricted, vibrato-laden female voice with glottal ornaments
Dry clicking phách rhythm under twangy đàn đáy lute
Occasional praise-drum strokes from a seated connoisseur

name: Quan họ
sound: Alternating love-song duets from the villages of Bắc Ninh: a pair of women answers a pair of men from another village, singing close, ornamented melodies that were traditionally unaccompanied and are now often staged with folk instruments.
markers: Two women answer two men in turn, the pair singing together
Dense vocal ornaments and vowel fillers (i hi, ư hư) around the lyric
Old form unaccompanied; modern staged form adds đàn nguyệt, đàn bầu, flute and fiddle

name: Bihu songs (Bihu geet)
tradition: Indian regional folk and Punjabi music
sound: Spring festival song of Assam: bright call-and-response love and nature verses driven by dhol, the buffalo-horn pepa, gogona and toka, now also sung on yearly Rongali Bihu albums.
markers: Dhol drumming with pepa (buffalo-horn pipe), gogona, toka and flute
Short teasing love and spring couplets, often call-and-response
Released in time for Rongali Bihu in mid-April

name: Thai classical (piphat and mahori)
sound: Siamese court and temple music: loud piphat ensembles of gong circles, xylophones and the oboe-like pi, and the softer mahori with strings, playing layered variations of one melody in a seven-tone equal tuning.
markers: Gong circles and xylophones in heterophony
Seven-tone, near-equal tuning
Small ching cymbals marking the cycle

name: Hausa court and praise music (kakaki, goge, maroka)
sound: Music of the Hausa emirates: kakaki trumpets and kettledrums for the emir, and praise singers with goge fiddle, kalangu talking drum or kuntigi lute naming and praising patrons.
markers: Long kakaki trumpet blasts over kettledrums
Rasping one-string goge fiddle
Call-and-response praise naming the patron

name: Pungmul (nongak)
sound: Korean village music: loud outdoor bands of gongs and drums driving dancers in cycling rhythms, and folk songs sung with bending, sobbing voices over an hourglass drum.
markers: Small kkwaenggwari gong leading janggu, buk and jing in accelerating cycles
Swung triple-feel rhythms that speed up to a frenzy
Solo voice with wide vibrato and call-and-response refrains, as in Arirang

name: Hua'er
years: c. 1368 onward (Ming dynasty; recorded from the 20th century)
sound: Northwest Chinese mountain love song of Gansu, Qinghai and Ningxia: a high, ringing, usually unaccompanied voice singing improvised couplets to named tunes (ling), shared by Hui, Han, Tu, Salar, Dongxiang, Bonan and Tibetan singers.
markers: One high, open-throated voice, usually unaccompanied
Tunes named as 'ling' after towns, peoples or flowers
Improvised love verses opening on a mountain or flower image

name: Kulintang
sound: Gong-chime music of the Muslim southern Philippines and neighbouring islands: a row of eight small knobbed gongs plays the melody over big hanging agung gongs, gandingan gongs and a goblet drum locked in fast, driving rhythmic modes.
markers: A bright row of small kettle gongs carrying the tune
Deep hanging agung and gandingan gongs answering in a repeating pattern
Named rhythmic modes (binalig, duyog, sinulog, tidtu) driven by a single drum

name: Malhun
years: 15th century onward (from the Tafilalt oases; later the song of Meknes, Fes, Salé, Marrakech)
sound: Moroccan sung poetry: a long strophic poem (qasida) in dialectal Arabic, sung by a lead voice with a refrain (harba) taken up between verses, over lute, violin, rebab and small drums.
markers: Long strophic poem in Moroccan dialectal Arabic, words first
A refrain (harba) answered between the verses
Lute, violin, rebab and small hand drums

name: Turkish folk song (türkü and âşık saz)
sound: Anatolian village and minstrel song: the long-necked bağlama (saz) under a declaimed or ornamented voice, from Alevi âşık poetry to the regional türküler of radio and the türkü bar.
markers: Bağlama saz drone and strummed riffs
Uneven aksak rhythms such as 9/8, or free-time bozlak
Mystic, philosophical or lament lyrics

name: Garba and dandiya raas
tradition: Indian regional folk and Punjabi music
sound: Gujarat's Navratri circle-dance song: devotional and Krishna songs to the Mother goddess, sung by a lead voice over dhol and clapping as dancers circle a lamp-lit pot or clash dandiya sticks.
markers: Dhol or dholak driving a looping dance beat, with handclaps or clicking sticks
Gujarati verses to Amba or about Radha and Krishna, with a short refrain
Songs run together in long non-stop medleys that speed up through the night

name: Sikh gurbani kirtan
sound: Singing of the Sikh scripture in its prescribed ragas: a lead ragi with harmonium and tabla, the congregation answering, from the Golden Temple's daily round to diaspora gurdwaras.
markers: Harmonium and tabla under a lead voice
Raga-set shabads with a sung refrain (rahao)
Punjabi and Braj scripture texts

name: Kazakh and Kyrgyz akyn song (aitys, zhyr, än)
sound: Sung poetry of the Kazakh and Kyrgyz steppe: epic chanting by zhyraus and manaschis, improvised verse duels between akyns, and lyric songs, carried by one voice and a dombra or komuz.
markers: Dombra or komuz strummed under the voice
Improvised rhymed verse, often a two-singer duel
Throaty epic recitation or soaring lyric melody

name: Mahagita (Burmese classical song)
years: 16th century onward (oldest kyo songs late Ava era; anthologised from c. 1788; standard edition 1954–61)
sound: The Burmese court's classical song repertoire: a solo singer, usually a woman, unfolding long ornamented lines of court poetry over the arched saung harp or a small chamber ensemble, in kyo, bwe, thachingan, patpyo and Thai-derived yodaya forms.
markers: A single voice closely shadowed by the saung harp (or piano, xylophone)
Small bell and clapper (si and wa) quietly marking the cycle
Slow, restrained court poetry about kings, the Buddha, forests and longing

name: Sufi kafi (Punjabi, Saraiki and Sindhi)
tradition: Indian regional folk and Punjabi music
sound: Sung Sufi poetry of Shah Hussain, Bulleh Shah and Khwaja Ghulam Farid: a solo voice with a refrain, over harmonium, tabla or dholak, building from slow longing to ecstatic repetition.
markers: Solo voice returning to a short refrain
Harmonium and tabla or dholak
Punjabi or Saraiki mystic verse of divine love

name: Arabian Peninsula folk (ardah, samri, fijiri)
sound: Bedouin and Gulf-coast song and dance: massed male chorus and frame drums in the ardah sword dance, clapping samri, and the pearl divers' fijiri with its low, groaning chant.
markers: Call-and-response male chorus
Frame drums and hand-claps in cross-rhythm
Slow modal melody, sometimes with oud or rababa

name: Kobzar dumy (Ukrainian epic song)
sound: Ukrainian Cossack-era epic laments, half-sung, half-recited by blind wandering kobzari and lirnyky to their own bandura, kobza or lira (hurdy-gurdy), telling of captives in Turkish slavery, dying Cossacks and broken families.
markers: One voice with bandura, kobza or the droning lira
Free, recitative lines with no fixed verse, ending in long sighing cadences
Stories of Turkish captivity, Cossack deaths and a widow's sons

name: Tarantella
years: c. 1600 onward (recorded from the 1950s; revival from the 1970s)
sound: Southern Italian folk dance music in a fast, driving 6/8 or 12/8, led by frame drums with organetto, fiddle, guitar, mandolin or bagpipe, in local forms such as the Salento pizzica, the Campanian tammurriata and the tarantellas of Calabria and Montemarano.
markers: Relentless frame-drum pulse (tamburello or the big tammorra) in a fast triplet swing
Organetto, violin, mandolin or zampogna repeating short dance phrases
Dialect singing, often a solo voice and chorus, that speeds up for the dancers

name: Iraqi maqam
years: c. 1600 onward (roots in Abbasid Baghdad; recorded from at least 1932)
sound: Baghdad's classical vocal suite: a lead singer (qāri') improvises long, ornate verses in a set mode against the chalghi ensemble of santur, joza spike fiddle, dumbak and daff, and each maqam ends in a lighter folk song, the pesteh.
markers: Hammered santur and scratchy joza fiddle, light hand drums
One male or female voice, long unmetred melismatic lines in classical and colloquial Arabic
A slow free maqam that breaks into a bouncy pesteh song at the end

name: Pashto folk song (charbeta, tappa)
sound: The village and hujra song of the Pashtuns of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and eastern and southern Afghanistan: two-line tappa verses and fast, chorus-answered charbeta epics, sung over rubab, harmonium, mangai pot drum or tabla and dhol.
markers: Short two-line tappa verses, the second line longer than the first
Bright rubab runs over a driving pot-drum or dhol beat
In charbeta, a fast lead line answered by a chorus

name: Bhawaiya and bhatiali
sound: Folk song of the Bengal countryside in two strands: bhawaiya from Rangpur, Cooch Behar and Goalpara, sung over the two-string dotara about cart drivers, buffalo herders and women left waiting, and bhatiali, the boatmen's song of the river delta, sung freely in long, high, drawn-out lines.
markers: Long, drawn-out melancholy vocal lines
Two-string dotara accompaniment
Bouncy, skipping chatka songs alongside the slow ones

name: Hsaing waing
years: 1600 onward (first pictured in the 1600s; recorded from the 1950s)
sound: Burma's loud outdoor ensemble for theatre, puppet plays, Buddhist ceremonies and spirit rites: a leader seated inside a ring of 21 tuned drums plays the tune with a gong circle, gong chime and a nasal hne oboe, all in heterophony over bell and clapper.
markers: A circle of tuned drums carrying the melody in fast virtuoso runs
Bronze gong circle and a shrill double-reed oboe doubling the tune
Sudden lurches in tempo and rhythm, held together by a small bell and clapper

name: Zapin and joget
years: zapin from about the 14th century, joget from the colonial era in Malacca (recorded from 1931)
sound: Malay social-dance music of the Straits: zapin pairs the gambus lute and interlocking marwas frame drums with sung pantun verses, often opened by a free gambus solo; joget is quicker, a violin over gong and rebana with a teasing lilt that plays twos against threes.
markers: Gambus lute leading, often opening with a free, unmetered solo
Interlocking marwas frame drums driving the zapin beat between sung verses
A quick joget violin over gong and rebana, beats felt in twos and threes at once

name: Zarzuela
sound: Spanish musical theatre that alternates spoken scenes with sung numbers, mixing operatic voices with Spanish popular song and dance. It flourished from the 1850s to the 1930s.
markers: Operatic voices singing in Spanish
Spoken dialogue between numbers
Spanish dance rhythms: jota, seguidilla, chotis, habanera

name: Levantine dabke
sound: Village line-dance music of the Levant: the double-reed mijwiz and tabl drum drive the stamping steps, and a singer calls out verses that the dancers answer.
markers: Buzzing mijwiz or, today, a synth playing its lines
Heavy stamping drum pattern
Call-and-response wedding verses

name: Irish and Scottish dance music (reels, jigs, céilí, Cape Breton)
sound: Instrumental dance tunes of Ireland and Scotland (reels, jigs, hornpipes, strathspeys) on fiddle, pipes, flute and accordion, later massed in céilí bands and carried to Cape Breton and America.
markers: Fast reels and jigs played in sets of two or three tunes
Fiddle, uilleann pipes, flute and button accordion
Ornamented melody over bodhrán, guitar or piano vamp

name: Maracatu
years: c. 1700 onward (first written record 1711; recorded on album from the 1990s)
sound: Afro-Brazilian carnival processional music of Pernambuco: massed rope-tuned alfaia bass drums, snares and a gonguê bell under call-and-response songs (loas) in the urban baque virado of Recife and Olinda nations, and a faster, brass-led baque solto in the rural Mata Norte form.
markers: A wall of heavy alfaia bass drums playing interlocking, syncopated patterns
A clanging gonguê bell and rattling abê shakers riding over the drums
A solo singer answered by a chorus in short, repeated loas

name: Currulao (Pacific marimba music)
years: c. 1700 onward (recorded from at least the 1970s)
sound: Afro-descendant marimba music of the southern Pacific coast of Colombia and Esmeraldas in Ecuador: a chonta-wood marimba over bamboo resonators leads two bombo bass drums, two cununo hand drums and guasá shakers, while women cantadoras answer a lead voice in rough three-part harmony.
markers: A wooden chonta marimba with a low ostinato and a high improvising part
Deep bombos and slapped cununos in a rolling 6/8
Call-and-response between a lead singer and a chorus of women shaking guasás

name: Jota
years: c. 1700 onward (named from the 18th century; recorded on 78s from the early 20th century, in the field by Alan Lomax in 1952, revived by folk groups from the 1970s)
sound: Spain's most widespread folk song and dance, strongest in Aragon: a fast triple-time dance played by a rondalla of bandurrias, lutes and guitars with castanets, framing a slow, ornamented solo verse sung at full voice; other regions play it on dulzaina and drum, bagpipes or tambourines.
markers: Brisk 3/4 or 3/8 lilt in a major key, swinging between tonic and dominant seventh
Bandurria and lute melody over strummed guitars and clicking castanets
A powerful solo voice slowing down for an ornamented eight-syllable quatrain

name: Hardanger fiddle and bygdedans (slåtter)
years: c. 1700 onward (the oldest surviving Hardanger fiddle is from 1651; recorded on 78s by the 1920s)
sound: Solo fiddle dance music of southern and western Norway played on the Hardanger fiddle, whose sympathetic understrings ring under constant double-stopping, in local tunings, for the bygdedans: gangar, springar and the acrobatic halling, plus listening pieces (lydarslåttar) and bridal marches.
markers: Shimmering drone from sympathetic strings under two-string bowing
Springar in an uneven three-beat pulse that differs from valley to valley
Fiddler's foot stamping the beat, solo and unaccompanied

name: Sa'idi music
years: c. 1700 onward (tree date; no page read dates the start: the Mataqil musician family goes back seven generations; first recordings found 1976)
sound: The folk music of Upper Egypt (the Sa'id, around Luxor), played by hereditary musician clans at weddings and mawlids: the two-string rababa fiddle with darbuka and duff behind folk songs, mawwal and the Hilali epic, and the mizmar sa'idi shawm band with the double-headed tabl baladi that drives the tahtib stick dance.
markers: A piercing mizmar shawm played with circular breathing, often two or three at once
A booming tabl baladi bass drum beating heavy dum against fast tak strokes
A two-string rababa fiddle trilling around a rough solo voice

name: Lavani
years: Beginnings traced to the 1560s; prominent in the late Peshwa era (poet-singers such as Ram Joshi, 1762–1812, and Honaji Bala); on record through Marathi tamasha films from 1947 and still current (film lavanis of 2010 and 2022).
tradition: Indian regional folk and Punjabi music
sound: Marathi song-and-dance of the tamasha stage: a woman singer, often in a quick tempo, over the powerful rhythm of the dholki drum, singing of love, longing and flirtation. The public stage form is phadachi lavani; the seated, private baithakichi lavani is sung before a small audience, and Honaji Bala brought the tabla in place of the dholki.
markers: A driving dholki drum rhythm under the voice
A woman singer in a quick tempo, teasing and flirtatious
Songs of love and longing for an absent or reluctant lover

name: Uzbek folk and classical song (katta ashula, lapar, dutar song)
sound: Uzbek song outside the full maqom suites: Fergana katta ashula sung into a tray, playful lapar dialogues, and dutar- and doira-accompanied folk and wedding songs.
markers: Dutar or doira accompaniment
Soaring, ornamented melisma in the high register
Wedding and work-song refrains such as yor-yor

name: Sega
sound: Creole dance song of Mauritius, Réunion and the Seychelles, born among enslaved Africans and Malagasy: a swaying 6/8 on ravanne frame drum, shaker and triangle, later with guitars and keyboards.
markers: Rolling 6/8 on the ravanne frame drum
Maravanne shaker and triangle keeping time
Creole lyrics, teasing or lamenting, with chorus replies

name: Maloya
years: 18th century onward (born among the enslaved; banned until 1981; first public performance 1959, on record from 1972)
sound: Réunion's slave-descended music, sung in Réunion Creole: a solo voice answered by a chorus over a rolling ternary beat from the roulèr barrel drum, the kayamb rattle, piker and sati idiophones and the bobre musical bow; sacred forms in the servis kabaré ancestor rites, secular forms at the kabar, and since the late 1970s also electric versions with guitar, bass and keyboards.
markers: A low roulèr barrel drum, played with both hands, rolling in a ternary pulse
The swish of the kayamb rattle and the struck twang of the bobre musical bow
A solo singer answered by a chorus in Réunion Creole

name: Rara
sound: Haitian street-procession music of Lent and Easter week, best known from Léogâne: bands of single-note bamboo trumpets (vaksin) play interlocking hocket patterns, tapping the tubes with sticks, over strapped marching drums, tin konet horns, scrapers, maracas and rattles made of recycled metal, while singers lead satirical, double-meaning songs in Haitian Creole; Haitian cane workers carry it into the Dominican Republic as gagá.
markers: Single-note bamboo vaksin trumpets locking together in a looping hocket, tapped with sticks
Marching drums, tin horns, scrapers and rattles heard moving down a road
A crowd chorus singing teasing, double-meaning songs in Haitian Creole

name: Huapango (son huasteco)
years: Roots in colonial-era son (18th century, Sierra Huasteca); the son huasteco as now played dates from the 19th century, with the violin-jarana-huapanguera trio standard from the 1950s; on record from the 1960s (earliest verified album 1966) to today.
sound: String-trio music of La Huasteca in northeastern Mexico: a virtuoso, flamboyant violin leads, the deep five-course huapanguera and the small jarana huasteca strum a rhythm that mixes duple and triple metre, and two singers trade improvised and traditional coplas in high voices with falsetto breaks while the violin falls silent and dancers' zapateado softens.
markers: High duet singing with sudden falsetto breaks
Ornate, improvised violin runs between the sung verses
Strummed jarana and deep huapanguera in a lilting rhythm that shifts between 3 and 2 feel

name: Verbunkos
years: c. 1760 onward (took shape in the second half of the 18th century, first known printed piece 1784, played at recruiting until conscription in 1848–49; recorded by Hungarian Gypsy bands from the 1950s and kept alive as a village men's dance and in the táncház revival)
sound: Hungarian recruiting-dance music: a proud, slow lassú in sharp dotted rhythm followed by a fast friss of virtuosic running notes, played by Romani bands of violins and cimbalom with ornamented violin figures and augmented-second turns; the ancestor of the csárdás, still danced in villages as the men's verbunk.
markers: A slow, proud lassú in short-long dotted rhythm that breaks into a fast, running friss
Lead violin spinning ornamented runs over a Gypsy band of strings and cimbalom
Augmented-second and diminished-seventh turns in a major or minor melody

name: Sevdalinka and starogradska (Bosnian and Yugoslav urban song)
sound: Slow, ornamented Bosnian love songs in Ottoman-tinged modes, sung with deep longing over saz and later accordion, violin and small kafana bands; starogradska is its gentler, Central European-leaning cousin.
markers: Long melismatic phrases on single vowels
Augmented-second Ottoman modes
Accordion or saz with violin

name: Morna
sound: Cape Verde's national song: slow, minor-key and full of sodade, sung in Creole over guitar, cavaquinho, violin and clarinet.
markers: Slow, swaying tempo and minor-key melody
Guitar and cavaquinho with violin or clarinet replies
Creole lyrics of longing, emigration and the sea

name: Morenada and diablada
years: c. 1790 onward (scores from the 1860s; first organised diablada troupe 1904; brass-band diablada in Puno from 1962; on record from the 1960s)
sound: The brass-band dance music of the Oruro Carnival and the Andean fiestas of Bolivia, Peru's Puno and northern Chile. The morenada is a slow, heavy dance march for trumpets, tubas, bass drum and cymbals, with the dancers' matraca rattles grinding over it. The diablada, the devil dance, comes in two parts: a march, then the devil's mecapaqueña. Both were once played on sikus and are now played by bronze bands; Oruro alone has about 150 bands. Andean folk groups also record both as named pieces.
markers: A slow, heavy, swaying march beat on bass drum and cymbals
Massed trumpets, horns and tubas playing the tune together
The rasping crank of matraca rattles over the band

name: Sevillanas
years: c. 1800 onward (seguidillas danced in Seville since the late 16th century, a distinct dance from the 18th; the modern form arose with the Seville Fair in the later 19th century; 78s from the 1920s, the first records by sevillanas groups from 1950, the boom of 1983-1988)
sound: Seville's festive couple dance song: always a set of four sevillanas in triple time, each a seven-line copla (a seguidilla and a refrain) sung over strummed guitar, palmas and often castanets, the music and the dancers stopping together at the close. The rociera kind for the El Rocío pilgrimage adds the pipe and tabor and, with the Rocío choirs, choral harmony; from the 1960s dedicated vocal groups, bass, electric instruments and orchestral arrangements came in. It borrows flamenco's colour but is not a flamenco palo.
markers: Strummed guitar introduction, then a brisk triple-time beat of palmas and castanets
Four short coplas to a set, music and dancers ending together on the last one
Group voices in harmony singing of Seville, Triana, the Feria and the road to El Rocío

name: Dohori
years: Village sung duels from at least the 19th century (no source gives a year); on Radio Nepal and record from the late 1970s and 1980s; a commercial cassette, VCD and YouTube industry from the late 1990s, after Nepal Television's 'Lok Dohori' programme (1998) and the dohori sanjh restaurants
sound: Nepal's sung duel: two sides, usually young men against young women, trade improvised rhyming couplets as question and answer over the repeated tune and refrain of a well-known folk song, to the beat of the madal drum, often with harmonium and sarangi; rooted in the Gurung rodhi ghar courting evenings of the central hills, and on record a lively, tightly arranged male-female duet whose lyrics move from love and teasing to migration, politics and Tij-festival protest.
markers: A male and a female voice answering each other couplet by couplet, each reply rhymed to the last
One repeated folk tune and refrain carrying many verses, the lyric changing with each question and answer
The madal hand drum driving a dancing beat, with harmonium or sarangi filling between couplets
Teasing, witty Nepali verse full of place names, proverbs, plants and animals used for the rhyme

name: Tamang selo
years: c. 1800 onward (tree date; no page read dates the start). First recordings: Hira Devi Waiba's Radio Nepal songs of 1966 and HMV albums of 1974 and 1978; cassette albums from the 1990s; a large flow of digital singles 2023 onward.
sound: The song and dance of the Tamang people of the hills around the Kathmandu Valley (Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Sindhupalchok, Kavre) and of the Nepali-speaking hills of Darjeeling and Sikkim: a brisk, rhythmic folk song driven by the damphu frame drum with madal and the tungna lute, sung for Lhosar, weddings and gatherings about love, sorrow, humour and everyday life, often as a call between singers, and since the 1990s also set to drum kit, guitar and keyboards in Nepali pop.
markers: The damphu, a large tambourine-like frame drum with 32 pegs, setting a bouncing dance pulse
Madal hand drum and the plucked tungna lute beside the damphu
Short, catchy sung verses about love, sorrow and village life, lively or slow, often traded between a man and a woman
Tamang words and names in the lyrics (maichyang, chyangba, syangbo) and Lhosar themes

name: Bambuco
sound: The song and dance of the Colombian Andes: a lilting rhythm that slips between 3/4 and 6/8, sung in two-voice duets over tiple, guitar and bandola.
markers: Syncopated sway between 3/4 and 6/8
Tiple, guitar and bandola strings
Two voices in parallel thirds, nostalgic lyrics

name: Pasillo
years: c. 1830 onward (tree date; pages read put its birth in the first decades of the 19th century, in the Andes of New Granada during the independence wars; in Ecuador from the 1870s; the sung pasillo from the 1910s; still recorded in 2026)
sound: A fast or slow song and dance in 3/4 adapted from the European waltz in Colombia and Ecuador. In Colombia it is either an instrumental pasillo fiestero for bandola, tiple and guitar (or piano) with spoon percussion, or a slow sung pasillo for two voices with string accompaniment. In Ecuador it became the national song: slow, melancholic, in low keys, setting modernist poems about lost love, sung by duets and later trios with requinto guitar.
markers: Three-beat (3/4) waltz time, quick and dance-like in Colombia, slow and dragging in Ecuador
Two voices in parallel thirds over guitars, or an instrumental lead on bandola, tiple or piano
Ecuadorian pasillos: a slow, mournful minor-key melody setting a poem of loss and longing
Colombian pasillo fiestero: quick instrumental dance pieces with spoon (cucharas) percussion

name: Magyar nóta (Hungarian popular song)
sound: Composed Hungarian songs in a folk-like style, sung in cafés and restaurants over a Gypsy orchestra: slow, free-rhythm laments that turn into fast csárdás.
markers: Lead violin and cimbalom shadowing the singer
Slow rubato verse, then a quick csárdás
Sentimental words of love, wine and home

name: Haitian méringue (mereng)
years: c. 1850 onward (tree date; English Wikipedia gives mid-19th century; earliest recordings found are the Lomax field recordings of 1936-37; largely absorbed into kompa from the mid-1950s)
sound: Haiti's national song and dance: a lilting, unhurried couple dance in duple time built on the five-note quintolet (the Cuban cinquillo, 'dak-ta-dak-ta-dak'), played on strings, piano and horns rather than the Dominican accordion and sung in Haitian Creole or French. It ranges from the slow, caressing salon or concert méringue for solo piano (Lamothe, the Duroseaus), through the quicker dance méringue of the 1940s-50s Port-au-Prince orchestras, to the excited, satirical carnival méringue.
markers: The five-note quintolet / cinquillo figure (long-short-long-short-long) running under the melody
Strings, piano and horns, not accordion: guitar and saxophone orchestras or a solo salon piano
A slower, swaying, nostalgic tempo than Dominican merengue, with Creole or French vocals

name: Gaita zuliana
years: 1850 onward (tree date; es.wikipedia places the origins perhaps in the first decades of the 19th century; first recordings in the late 1940s, national popularity from the 1960s)
sound: The Christmas-season song of Zulia state, Venezuela: a solo singer trades four-line coplas with a mixed chorus singing the estribillo over a 6/8 swing, carried by the cuatro, the friction drum furro (furruco) as bass, maracas, the metal scraper charrasca and the tambora; sung to the Virgin of Chiquinquirá, to Maracaibo and in protest, from the 1960s conjuntos to the tamborera and salsa-touched bands of the 1970s.
markers: A furro friction drum giving a groaning bass pulse
Strummed cuatro and the rasping metal charrasca on a 6/8 swing
A solo copla answered by a full mixed-voice chorus
Lyrics to the Virgin of Chiquinquirá, Maracaibo and political protest

name: Pasodoble
years: c. 1850 onward (tree date; Spanish Wikipedia dates pasodoble scores to 1780 as an infantry march and puts it in the bullring only in the 19th century; the oldest piece here, La Gracia de Dios, is from 1880; the first recordings found are España cañí by the Banda del Regimiento de Ingenieros de Madrid, 1926)
sound: Spain's quick march in binary time, played by bandas de música in the bullring, in Moros y Cristianos and Fallas parades and at village dances: an introduction on the dominant, a first strain in the home key and a 'trío' that comes back loud to close, often with an Andalusian, flamenco-tinged turn. Taurino pasodobles are the slowest, popular ones the fastest, and from the 1910s copla singers sang it as the pasodoble canción about toreros, Andalusia and Spain.
markers: A brisk two-beat march pulse (binary time, one step per beat) from a full wind band with snare and bass drum
Introduction, a first strain in the home key, then a 'trío' that is replayed loud as the climax
An Andalusian, flamenco-tinged melody, often in a minor key (Suspiros de España)
In the sung pasodoble canción, a copla singer telling of toreros, bullfights and Andalusian or Spanish pride over the same march beat

name: Harana (serenade)
years: From the 1800s (Spanish era; the tree's 1850 is a judgement, no source gives a year); at its height before the Second World War and on 1940s-50s radio and records; the custom has declined since the 1980s and lives on in revival recordings (The Art of Harana 2003, the Harana Kings 2012).
sound: The Filipino courtship serenade: a young man, often with friends, sings love songs under a woman's window at night to his own or a companion's guitar. The songs are mostly danzas in a 2/4 habanera rhythm and a major key, opened by a solo guitar introduction with a guitar interlude between verses, in pure and archaic Tagalog (or Ilocano, Cebuano and other languages) that places the singer in the act of serenading. Haranistas also sang kundiman, which is a related but distinct 3/4 art song.
markers: A lilting 2/4 habanera (danza) rhythm on one or two guitars
A solo guitar introduction and a guitar interlude between the verses
A lone tender male voice, crooning, addressing a beloved at her window at night
Lyrics in old-fashioned, formal Tagalog or another Philippine language, pleading for love

name: Jiangnan sizhu (silk and bamboo)
years: 1860 onward (Chinese Wikipedia: in vogue from 1860; Shanghai the centre by the early 20th century; the name fixed in the 1950s); still played by amateur clubs and conservatories
sound: The amateur instrumental ensemble music of the lower Yangzi (southern Jiangsu, Shanghai, northern Zhejiang), played in teahouses and music clubs: a small, unfixed group of silk strings and bamboo winds (erhu, the long qudi flute or xiao, pipa and yangqin at the core, with sanxian, qinqin, sheng and a clapper) works a small body of old melodies, above all the Eight Great Pieces, each player ornamenting the same tune in a gentle heterophony where one fills in as another thins out.
markers: A soft, legato qudi or xiao flute and an erhu sharing the lead in the same melody
Heterophony: pipa, yangqin and sanxian each decorate one tune at once ("you busy, me simple")
One old melody heard in plain, slow and ornamented forms (Lao liu ban, Man liu ban, Zhong hua liu ban)
Chamber scale: two to ten players, one of each instrument, only a clapper and small drum for percussion

name: Bal-musette (Paris accordion dance music)
sound: Paris dance-hall music where Auvergnat bagpipe dances met Italian accordionists: quick valses, javas and polkas on a bright, wavering accordion, later swung by Manouche guitarists.
markers: Wet, tremolo 'musette' accordion tuning
Fast valse musette and the lurching java
Banjo or guitar chugging behind

name: Gambang kromong
years: Mid-18th century beginnings (Kapitan Nie Hoe Kong, in office 1736–1740) as a gambang orchestra; named gambang kromong once the kromong was added in the early 20th century; peak of popularity around 1937; still played across greater Jakarta, on record in Benyamin S. and Ida Royani's Betawi songs, 1990s cassettes, the Smithsonian Folkways field album of 1991 and digital releases to 2024.
sound: The orchestra of Jakarta's Betawi and Chinese-Peranakan communities: the wooden gambang xylophone and the kromong gong-chime with gong, kendang drums, suling flute and kecrek, under the Chinese bowed strings sukong, tehyan and kongahyan carrying the melody, in a Chinese pentatonic scale. Its repertoire runs from instrumental phobin and classical lagu dalem sung by cokek singers to the popular lagu sayur (Jali-Jali, Stambul, Cente Manis) for cokek dancing and lenong theatre; 'gambang kromong kombinasi' adds guitar, bass, organ, saxophone and drums.
markers: The nasal, sliding melody of the Chinese two-string fiddles (tehyan, kongahyan, sukong) over a wooden xylophone
The ringing kromong gong-chime and gong marking the cycle, with kendang drum for dancing
A Chinese pentatonic tune sung in Betawi Malay, often a playful pantun-style lagu sayur such as Jali-Jali or a Stambul

name: Shōka and gunka (school and military songs)
years: 1881 to 1945: from the first Ministry of Education school songbook (Shōgaku shōkashū, first volume dated 1881) and one of the first composed gunka (Battōtai, 1885) to Japan's surrender. Monbushō shōka filled school textbooks from 1910 to 1944 (the subject itself became 'music' in 1941); gunka boomed in the wars of 1894-95 and 1904-05 and were mass-produced on records from 1931, then banned under the Occupation until 1952. Re-recorded by choirs and singers ever since.
sound: The Western-style songs Meiji Japan built for its schools and its army: simple, singable melodies in a major key, at first borrowed from German and American school songs, hymns and Scottish airs and given Japanese words, then newly composed by Japanese musicians from 1910. School shōka are sung by children's or mixed choirs with piano or small orchestra, about the seasons, the home village and diligence; gunka are marching songs in four-four time with a brass band of trumpets, trombones, snare and cymbals behind unison male voices, telling the story of a battle or a fallen comrade, and from the 1930s they became record-company hits with star singers.
markers: Plain major-key tunes that a whole class or regiment can sing in unison, many on the five-note yonanuki scale
Children's or mixed choir with piano or small orchestra for school songs; unison male voices over a military brass band in march time for gunka
Long strophic texts in formal literary Japanese: the seasons and the home village, or a battle, a hero and a dead comrade, verse after verse

name: Nurthi
years: 1879 onward (C. Don Bastian's Rolina, per the Sunday Times; the tree's 1886 is John de Silva's Ramayanaya per English Wikipedia); commercial nurthi stage ended with silent cinema (no year read); revived from 1978 at the restored Tower Hall and by the Tower Hall Theatre Foundation
sound: The song of the Sinhala nurthi stage, a musical theatre born in Colombo from the Parsi touring companies (Elphinstone Dramatic Company, 1880s): Sinhala verses set to Hindustani and Gujarati stage melodies, with raga and tala chosen to fit each scene's sentiment (rasa), accompanied by harmonium, violin and dhol. John de Silva's plays on Sinhala history and Buddhist legend (Siri Sangabo, 1903) gave its best-known songs, such as Danno Budunge.
markers: A North Indian (Hindustani or Parsi-theatre) melody carrying Sinhala verses
Harmonium leading, with violin and dhol drum behind the voice
Solo stage song in character from a play on kings, gods or Buddhist history, in a raga chosen for the scene's mood

name: Biguine
sound: Martinican dance-band music of Saint-Pierre and the Paris bals: clarinet, trombone and banjo or piano over a lilting, syncopated two-beat, with Creole lyrics.
markers: Clarinet lead weaving over the band
Bouncy syncopated 2/4 rhythm
Creole verses about love and town life

name: Meykhana
sound: Azerbaijani improvised rhymed verse from the villages around Baku: performers trade spoken-sung couplets on a set theme over a steady beat, now often with synths.
markers: Rapid, half-spoken rhymed couplets
Performers answering each other in turn
A fixed refrain line the crowd shouts back

name: Romanian folk and lăutărească (doina, hora, sârbă)
sound: Romanian village song and the urban lăutari tradition: free, ornamented doina laments and fast hora and sârbă dances on violin, cimbalom and accordion.
markers: Slow, unmetered doina with sobbing ornaments
Fast hora and sârbă dance rhythms
Violin, țambal and accordion bands

name: Funaná
years: c. 1900 onward (tree date; Wikipedia's oral tradition puts the accordion's arrival on Santiago at the start of the 20th century, with no document to prove it; the name dates from the 1960s-70s; first records found 1978)
sound: The accordion dance music of rural Santiago, Cape Verde: a diatonic button accordion (gaita) carrying the melody, bass and chords, a ferrinho iron scraper struck with a knife driving a fast two-beat pulse, and a Creole singer trading verses and refrain with accordion solos between them. Once banned in the colonial capital, it was electrified by Bulimundo around 1980 (guitar, bass, drums, synthesizer in place of the gaita), spread across the islands and abroad with Finaçon, and turned back to gaita and ferrinho with Ferro Gaita from 1997; danced in couples with quick alternating knee flexes.
markers: A diatonic button accordion (gaita) playing a running melody and solos between the verses
The scrape of a ferrinho iron bar struck with a knife on a fast two-beat pulse
A Creole singer trading proverb-laden verses with a refrain, in a tempo from andante to vivace

name: Porro
years: Band porro took shape in the Sinú and the savannas of Córdoba, Sucre and Bolívar in the late 19th century (the word 'porro' comes into use then; tree date 1900); orchestral porro spread nationally and abroad from the 1940s to the 1970s; band porro lives on in festivals (San Pelayo, since 1977) and in revival records (2010).
sound: Dance music of Colombia's Caribbean plains, born where gaita flute-and-drum groups met military wind bands: a banda pelayera of trumpets, clarinets, trombones and bombardino (euphonium) over bombo, snare and cymbals, in cut time (2/2). The trumpet leads the 'porro' section, the clarinet takes over in the 'bozá' while the bombo player beats a stick on the drum's rim (porro palitiao of the Sinú); in porro tapao of the savannas the bombo player muffles the far head with his hand. From the 1940s big orchestras such as Lucho Bermúdez's and Pacho Galán's dressed it for the ballroom.
markers: A brass band of trumpets, clarinets and bombardino trading call-and-response phrases
A bass drum (bombo) and snare driving a quick cut-time (2/2) march-like pulse, with cymbal crashes
A clarinet-led 'bozá' section over the dry click of a stick on the drum's rim
Instrumental or sung dance pieces for couples, often named after people and towns of Córdoba and Bolívar

name: Changga
years: 1896 to the late 1920s (the first changga of 1896; patriotic and school changga until about 1910, pushed underground by the colonial ban; yuhaeng changga, the popular songs of the 1920s, until the genres split in the 1930s)
sound: Korea's first Western-style songs: simple melodies in Western major and minor scales, very often borrowed (Protestant hymns, Scottish and American tunes such as Auld Lang Syne and Georgia March, Japan's Railway Song), set to Korean words in fixed syllable counts, 4·4 at first and 7·5 later, and sung verse after verse in unison by schoolchildren, church congregations and independence volunteers. Words urge study, strength and independence. In the 1920s yuhaeng changga carried the same plain melodic style into songs of parting and sorrow, such as 희망가 and the waltz 사의 찬미.
markers: A plain hymn-like or marching Western melody, often a borrowed foreign tune, sung in Korean
Many verses to one short tune, the lyrics in fixed syllable counts (4·4, later 7·5)
Words of exhortation, urging the young to study, grow strong and win independence (학도야 학도야), or in the 1920s a lament on a hard world

name: Russian folk song and folk choirs
sound: Village song staged for concert hall and radio: folk choirs, balalaika and domra orchestras, and big-voiced soloists singing laments, round dances and chastushki.
markers: Open-throated village singing in close harmony
Balalaika, domra and bayan accompaniment
Slow drawn-out songs and fast accelerating dances

name: Cải lương (Vietnamese reformed opera)
sound: Southern Vietnam's modern sung theatre: spoken drama broken by the slow, melismatic vọng cổ aria over đàn kìm and guitar with scooped frets.
markers: Vọng cổ: long, sliding vocal lines
Đàn kìm and scalloped-fret guitar
Spoken dialogue between sung verses

name: Schlager
sound: German-language popular song built for singing along: simple major-key melodies, sentimental or cheerful lyrics, and polished orchestral, later disco-pop, backing.
markers: Big, simple singalong chorus
Clean backing on a foxtrot, oom-pah or four-on-the-floor beat
Lyrics of love, longing, holidays and home

name: Russian chanson (blatnaya pesnya)
sound: Russian underworld and prison song: gravel-voiced story ballads over guitar, accordion or restaurant-band keyboards.
markers: Hoarse, conversational male vocal
Minor-key waltz or two-step with Odessa klezmer lilt
Stories of camps, thieves, mothers and lost freedom

name: Hebrew folk song (Shirei Eretz Yisrael) and army troupe song
sound: Hebrew songs of the Zionist settlement and early state: Russian- and Yiddish-tinged melodies, hora rhythms and Yemenite turns, sung by soloists, duos and army troupes.
markers: Unison communal singing, often accordion-led
Minor-key Russian-style melody or hora beat
Pastoral, patriotic Hebrew lyrics

name: Sudanese haqiba (hageeba)
years: 1920s onward (Omdurman's new urban song of the 1920s and 1930s, on Cairo-made 78s from the late 1920s; named 'haqiba' in the 1940s after Radio Omdurman's Hageebat al-Fann programme, and sung by later haqiba singers ever since)
sound: Omdurman's first secular urban song: a lead singer answered by a chorus, carried at first only by the riq or tar frame drum and handclaps, with melodies taken from madeeh praise singing and set to new love and homeland poems; pentatonic, close to Sufi praise chant in poetic form, sung at weddings and social gatherings, and from the late 1920s sometimes joined by violin, accordion or piano on record.
markers: A solo voice with a chorus that claps and echoes its main lines
Only the riq or tar frame drum and handclaps for accompaniment, no orchestra
Love and homeland poems sung to madeeh-derived pentatonic tunes

name: Twoubadou
years: Early 20th century onward (tree date 1920; no page gives a year). Kandjo (1879–1947) set the archetype; on record from Trio Select's first album in 1960; a commercial revival from the late 1990s (Mizik Mizik's Blakawout, Haitiando, Haiti Twoubadou) continues today.
sound: Haitian guitar-based song brought back from the Cuban cane fields by migrant cutters: one or two acoustic guitars, maracas or a graj scraper, a tanbou drum and a large lamellophone (manibula) playing the bass, with a pair of voices singing simple two-part verse-and-chorus songs about the bitterness and humour of love, often risqué. Played by small combos in clubs, restaurants, hotels and at patron-saint feasts, it sits close to Cuban son and mixes it with Haitian mereng.
markers: Two acoustic guitars trading Cuban-style lines over a light, swaying dance beat
Maracas or a graj scraper and a hand drum, with a thumb-piano (manibula) bass instead of a bass guitar
Two voices in Haitian Creole singing a short verse and a chorus about love, often teasing or suggestive

name: Soviet mass song (massovaya pesnya)
sound: State-backed songs for everyone to sing: marches, anthems and lyrical film and war songs by Dunayevsky, Blanter, Novikov and Solovyov-Sedoy, set for choir, orchestra or a crooner.
markers: Rousing choral or march refrains
Simple, singable tunes with a folk-like minor turn
Orchestral, brass or accordion accompaniment

name: Swedish visa and schlager (svensk visa och schlager)
sound: Swedish popular song from revue, radio and film: Evert Taube's sea-and-archipelago ballads beside waltz and foxtrot schlagers, sung in clear Swedish for the whole family.
markers: Clear, storytelling Swedish lyrics
Waltz, foxtrot or schottis under a light orchestra or guitar
Summer dances, the archipelago and the sea

name: Nazrul Geeti
sound: The several thousand songs of Kazi Nazrul Islam: Bengali lyrics set to raga and ghazal melody, ranging from love songs and Islamic devotional songs to marches of revolt.
markers: Bengali words on raga or ghazal-style melody
Harmonium and tabla, with ornamented, semi-classical singing
Persian and Arabic colour, or a marching beat in the patriotic songs

name: Chilean tonada and música típica
sound: Chile's huaso song: strummed guitars and close vocal harmony for tonadas and cuecas, polished by Santiago vocal groups for radio.
markers: Strummed guitars, often several
Close-harmony huaso vocal groups
Tonada lilt or cueca's 6/8 handclap

name: Samba-canção
sound: Samba slowed into a torch song for the radio age: the melody and the heartbreak lead, the rhythm softens, and strings or a small-hours piano take over from the percussion.
markers: Slow, muted samba pulse under a long melody
Big, dramatic radio voices or hushed nightclub crooning
Lyrics of betrayal, jealousy and lost love (dor de cotovelo)

name: Mexican bolero and trío romántico
sound: The Cuban bolero slowed and sweetened in Mexico: Agustín Lara's piano songs, then three-voice guitar trios with a high, picked requinto lead.
markers: Slow bolero pulse on guitars and maracas
Requinto guitar intro and fills
Close three-part harmony or a crooner over strings

name: Algerian chaâbi
sound: Popular song of the Algiers Casbah: long melhoun poems sung over mandole, banjo, violins and darbuka, slow and reflective, then breaking into a fast dance close.
markers: Mandole or banjo lead with violin unison
Long sung Arabic poems, often moral or about exile
Slow opening that speeds up at the end

name: Italian canzone (musica leggera)
sound: Italian light popular song from radio to the Sanremo festival: melodic, orchestral and sung for everyone, with a crooner's warmth and a big final chorus.
markers: Soaring, singable melody built for the chorus
Orchestra or beat combo behind a star voice
Standard Italian lyrics of love and longing

name: Finnish iskelmä and Finnish tango
sound: Finland's popular song: minor-key tangos, waltzes and foxtrots sung in Finnish by crooners over accordion, strings and dance band, plus translated European and American hits.
markers: Minor-key melody with a lyric of longing
Tango, waltz or humppa beat with accordion and strings
Big-voiced crooner or chanteuse singing in Finnish

name: Maskandi
sound: Zulu migrant-worker guitar music: a picked solo flourish, then a rolling groove with concertina, bass and rapid spoken praise poetry.
markers: Opening solo guitar flourish (izihlabo)
Fast spoken praise section (izibongo)
Fingerpicked guitar with concertina and call-and-response

name: Taiwanese Hokkien pop (Taiyu ge)
sound: Popular song in Taiwanese Hokkien: Japanese-era ballads, then enka-shaped songs of heartbreak, drink and the harbour, and later band and indie takes, in a language long squeezed off the airwaves.
markers: Enka-style vibrato and minor-key melody
Hokkien lyrics of hardship, love and the sea
Erhu, accordion or synth-string lines

name: Luk krung (Thai city song)
sound: Bangkok's urban song: Thai melodies sung with crooner polish over big-band and string arrangements, often in ballroom rhythms like the tango, cha-cha-chá and ramwong.
markers: Big-band brass and strings
Smooth, refined crooning with little ornament
Ballroom rhythms: ramwong, tango, cha-cha-chá

name: Tamil film music (Kollywood)
sound: South Indian film song from Madras: Carnatic-rooted melody fused with Tamil folk, Western orchestration and later synths, sung by playback singers for the Tamil screen.
markers: Playback singers over film orchestra or synths
Carnatic gamakas and Tamil folk rhythms
Bold mixes of Western pop, disco or reggae

name: Bengali modern song (adhunik gaan)
sound: Bengali popular song for records, radio and film: lyrical melodies for a solo voice over light orchestra, drawing on Tagore and Nazrul songs, Hindustani ragas and folk tunes.
markers: Warm, intimate lead vocal
Light orchestra with harmonium, strings and flute
Poetic Bengali lyrics

name: Marrabenta
sound: Maputo's urban dance music: bright, quick guitar picking over a skipping beat, sung in Ronga and Changana with call-and-response choruses.
markers: Fast, chiming guitar lines, first on home-made tin guitars
Skipping, forward-leaning dance beat
Call-and-response vocals in Ronga or Changana

name: Australian country and bush ballad
sound: Country music retold for the outback: plain-sung story songs about drovers, truckies, pubs and drought, growing out of hillbilly records and colonial bush songs.
markers: Story verses in a broad Australian accent
Pick-and-strum acoustic guitar, sometimes a yodel
Outback place names, stock work and dry humour

name: Sarala gee (Sinhala light song)
sound: Sinhala art song for radio: poetic lyrics on raga and folk-based melodies with sitar, tabla, violin and flute, shaped by composers who trained at Santiniketan and Lucknow.
markers: Gentle, raga-tinged Sinhala melody
Sitar, tabla, violin and bamboo flute
Literary lyrics, sung plainly without heavy ornament

name: Kabyle song
sound: Song in the Kabyle Berber language, from émigré-café chaabi to the guitar-led folk of the 1970s: poetic, often political, built on mandole, derbouka and call-and-response.
markers: Kabyle Berber lyrics, proverb-like poetry
Mandole or acoustic guitar over derbouka
Call-and-response choruses

name: Moroccan chaabi and aita
sound: Morocco's popular song for weddings and cassettes: the rural aita cry of the cheikhat and its urban chaabi offspring, on violin, loutar and hand drums.
markers: Shrill violin or loutar riffs
Driving bendir and taarija percussion
Raw, high women's voices and call-and-response

name: Sudanese popular song (golden age)
sound: Urban Sudanese song after haqiba: pentatonic melodies sung over oud, massed violins and accordion, later with electric guitar, horns and synths.
markers: Pentatonic melody, not Arabic maqam
Unison violins and accordion answering the singer
Loping tom-tom and bongo rhythms

name: Cuarteto
sound: Córdoba's own dance music: a relentless, bouncing 'tunga-tunga' two-beat from piano and bass, grown from immigrant pasodoble and tarantella bands and later sped up with merengue and tropical brass.
markers: Bouncing 'tunga-tunga' piano and bass two-beat
Accordion or keyboards and brass riffing over fast tempos
Shouted, party-leading vocals and crowd chants

name: Muzică ușoară (Romanian easy music)
sound: Romanian state-era light pop: melodic, danceable songs with radio-orchestra arrangements, close to schlager and Italian canzone.
markers: Big studio orchestra or pop band behind a clear solo voice
Romance-language lilt with Italian festival-song shape
Sentimental, censor-safe lyrics about love and seasons

name: Nhạc đỏ (red music)
sound: Vietnamese revolutionary song: marches and stirring ballads for the Việt Minh and North Vietnam, sung in trained, operatic voices.
markers: Bright, trained voices, solo or massed chorus
March rhythms or sweeping patriotic ballads
Lyrics of homeland, soldiers, Hồ Chí Minh and the front

name: Doo-wop
sound: Street-corner vocal group harmony: a high tenor lead over wordless backing syllables and a booming bass voice, singing teenage love songs.
markers: Nonsense-syllable backing vocals standing in for a band
Falsetto or high tenor lead against a deep bass voice
The I–vi–IV–V '50s progression' in slow triplets

name: Baila
sound: Sri Lankan party music from Afro-Portuguese kaffirinha roots: a bouncing 6/8 on guitars, bongos and keyboards, with comic or teasing Sinhala lyrics.
markers: Lilting 6/8 kaffirinha rhythm
Guitar and bongo dance-band sound
